scenario_stem:
ClearFlow Water Corporation is a public corporation owned by the Country X government, supplying tap water to 1.8 million households across 6 provinces. Founded in 1994, it employs 3,200 staff and records annual revenue of $420 million, but last year it required a government subsidy of $35 million to cover operating losses at its northern treatment plants.

The government proposes selling ClearFlow to a private investor group for $500 million, arguing the sale would clear part of its $900 million infrastructure debt and fund a $260 million modernisation programme. Private investors expect a profit margin of 12%, compared with ClearFlow's current 2%. Consumers fear water bills could rise by $8 per month, while the 3,200 employees worry about the 400 redundancies planned by the buyer.

questions.model_answer: A business organisation owned and controlled by the state or government, usually providing essential goods or services to the public. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Owned and controlled by the government or state

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To guarantee essential services to all citizens [k], ClearFlow supplies 1.8 million households across 6 provinces, including remote areas a private firm might avoid [app]. Reason 2: To keep water affordable [k], ClearFlow charges below cost and needed a $35 million subsidy last year rather than pursuing profit like a private owner would [app].

knowledge_max_2: Essential services provided to the whole population
Government controls prices to keep them affordable
application_max_2: Supplies 1.8 million households across 6 provinces

Problem 2: Employees may lose their jobs [k], because the buyer plans 400 redundancies among ClearFlow's 3,200 staff [app], cutting household incomes and weakening local communities [an].

analysis_max_2: Reduced disposable income may cause arrears

However, one argument against is that profit-seeking investors [k] would raise bills by $8 per month for 1.8 million households and cut 400 of ClearFlow's 3,200 staff [app], reducing affordability for low-income families and harming public welfare [an]. Overall, the government should not privatise ClearFlow [eval], because water is an essential service and the $35 million annual subsidy costs taxpayers far less than countrywide harm from higher bills and job losses [eval].

scenario_stem:
Aldermere City Transit is a bus service provided by Aldermere City Council, a local government authority, operating 45 buses across 12 routes in the town. Last year the service carried 2.4 million passenger journeys and cost $9.6 million to run, with fares covering only 60% of operating costs, so the council topped up $3.8 million from local taxes. It employs 210 drivers and maintenance staff.

A private operator, FastWay Coaches, has offered to run the network for $7.9 million a year, promising 8 newer buses and free Wi-Fi. In return it wants a 25% fare rise, authority to cut the 12 lowest-ridership routes serving rural suburbs, and exclusivity for 7 years. Councillors must decide by March whether to outsource the service, which carries 58,000 pensioners and students using concessionary fares each month.

questions.model_answer: An economy containing both a private sector and a public sector, where government and private businesses share the production of goods and services. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Contains both private and public sectors

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To serve areas private firms find unprofitable [k], Aldermere City Transit runs 12 routes covering rural suburbs where ridership is too low for FastWay Coaches to serve alone [app]. Reason 2: To keep transport affordable [k], fares cover only 60% of the $9.6 million cost, with a $3.8 million tax subsidy and concessionary fares for 58,000 pensioners and students [app].

Problem 2: 12 low-ridership routes would be cut [k], leaving rural suburbs without public transport despite the council's service objective [app], isolating elderly residents and raising their cost of reaching shops and hospitals [an].

However, one argument against is the harm to vulnerable passengers [k], since FastWay wants a 25% fare rise and to cut 12 rural routes, undermining the concessionary fares used by 58,000 pensioners and students [app], which conflicts with the council's duty to serve the whole community [an]. Overall, the council should not outsource now [eval], because a $1.7 million annual saving is outweighed by losing 12 routes and pricing out low-income residents, although it could negotiate better terms including fixed fares [eval].

scenario_stem:
Country X's care sector is part of a mixed economy combining private and public providers. Meridian Care Homes is a private company running 3 care homes with 120 beds in the capital, charging residents $1,450 per week and employing 78 qualified nurses and carers. Its waiting list is 25 names and its profit last year was $1.9 million.

The public National Care Trust operates a 200-bed facility in the same city, but its waiting list has grown to 340 people, with average waits of 9 months. The government, which spent $28 million on public care last year, is considering paying Meridian Care Homes $6 million to run 40 additional beds under contract, rather than build a new public ward costing $15 million.

However, one argument against is that public money would enrich a profit-making firm [k], whose $1,450 weekly fees and $1.9 million profit show a private objective that may conflict with affordable care for poorer residents [app], weakening long-term public provision [an]. scenario_stem:
Rivermart Stores PLC is a public limited company operating 26 supermarkets across Country X. It employs 1,900 people, reports annual revenue of $310 million and made a profit of $14 million last year, paying shareholders a dividend of $6 million. Opened 21 years ago, it is the country's third-largest supermarket chain. Managers have proposed automating checkouts in 18 stores, requiring a $6 million investment and cutting 150 jobs.

Employees, supported by their union, demand a pay rise of $0.75 per hour, costing about $2.9 million a year. Customers' groups want lower prices, while community groups want Rivermart to keep sourcing local produce from 120 farmers. At the next AGM, shareholders will vote on whether to approve the automation plan or the pay rise.

However, one argument against is the damage to stakeholder relations [k], since the union's $0.75 hourly claim costing $2.9 million is under half the automation spend, and cutting 150 of 1,900 staff would worsen morale [app], risking strikes, lost sales and reputational harm [an]. scenario_stem:
Nimbus Cycles Ltd is a bicycle retailer in Country X founded 2 years ago by Priya and Daniel. In its first year it made a loss of $25,000, and survival was its only objective. In year two it reached revenue of $480,000, made a profit of $40,000 and holds a 6% share of the city's bicycle market, with 9 employees.

Priya wants to open a second shop in the neighbouring town, costing $180,000, funded by a bank loan. Daniel argues the profit is too small to service the debt and wants to keep the objective of profit maximisation, rebuilding reserves which fell to $30,000. The first shop's rent is $4,200 per month, and sales of electric bikes grew by 45% last year.

Reason 2: A market opportunity exists [k], because electric-bike sales grew by 45% and its 6% share of the city market leaves room to win neighbouring-town customers [app].

However, one argument against is the financial risk of a $180,000 bank loan [k], because Priya and Daniel hold only $30,000 reserves and a $40,000 annual profit may not cover repayments if trade slows [app], threatening the original shop [an]. scenario_stem:
Orbit Phones Ltd is an established electronics retailer in Country X with 4 shops and an online store. Annual revenue is $24 million and its profit margin is 9%, earning about $2.16 million last year. Its market share is 14%, compared with TechZone's 22%, the market leader, and industry margins average 8%.

Marketing proposes a 10% price cut on 3,000 phone lines, which it predicts would lift market share to 18% within 12 months and sales volume by 25%. Finance calculates the cut would reduce profit by $1.8 million, leaving about $360,000. Suppliers have offered extended credit of $500,000 if Orbit commits to larger orders. The board meets next month to decide whether market share should replace profit as the main objective.

knowledge_max_2: Revenue minus total costs

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To close the gap with the market leader [k], because TechZone holds 22% and Orbit only 14%, so lifting share to 18% would strengthen its position in Country X [app]. Reason 2: Higher volume could secure cheaper supply [k], with suppliers offering $500,000 extended credit to win Orbit's larger orders if the 10% price cut proceeds [app].

Risk 2: A price war may follow [k], since rival TechZone with 22% share may cut its own prices to defend the lead [app], shrinking Orbit's revenue further below the $24 million baseline [an].

Rivals may retaliate with price cuts

questions.model_answer: One argument for pursuing market share is closing the gap with TechZone [k], since a 10% price cut could lift Orbit's share from 14% to 18% and sales volume by 25% across 3,000 lines [app], strengthening its long-term competitive position [an]. However, one argument against is the severe hit to profit [k], because Orbit's $2.16 million profit would fall by $1.8 million to about $360,000 on $24 million revenue [app], leaving little retained profit to fund growth or satisfy shareholders [an]. scenario_stem:
BrightPath Training is a private catering firm in Country X founded 5 years ago by Sofia Marchetti. It employs 14 chefs and waiters, and last year recorded revenue of $720,000 with a profit of $85,000, a margin of about 12%. Every weekend it runs cookery classes in schools for 60 disadvantaged teenagers, and revenue has grown by 30% over the last 3 years.

Sofia is deciding whether to convert BrightPath into a social enterprise with the objective of service to the community, reinvesting 70% of profits into free training for unemployed young people, or to keep chasing profit and pay herself a larger dividend. The directors estimate conversion would cut her annual dividend from $30,000 to $9,000 but could double the charity partners' funding.

Reason 2: It strengthens reputation and stakeholder support [k], because reinvesting 70% of profits could double charity partner funding and win community goodwill and local contracts [app].

scenario_stem:

It employs 7,500 staff, records revenue of $2.1 billion and received a government subsidy of $400 million last year. Average punctuality is 81%, fares have been frozen for 3 years and its workforce peaked at 8,000 in 2019.

The government faces two options, raise fares by 12% to cut the subsidy, or privatise CXNR to an overseas operator promising $700 million of investment and 5% service growth. scenario_stem:
In Country X's mixed economy, the StateSea ferry service is a public corporation crossing the Greywater Strait at a flat fare of $11, carrying 520,000 passengers a year on a government subsidy of $6 million. Its journey takes 70 minutes, 15 minutes longer than Harbourline's, and it employs 140 staff. StateSea was founded in 2009 and also holds the island mail contract worth $900,000 a year.
